newsitem.title: USA: Lawyer says U.S. hippie in France to fight extradition.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer says U.S. hippie in France to fight extradition.

text.p: The lawyer for a 1960s-era counterculture guru convicted in absentia of murder said on Wednesday his client has vowed to fight extradition from France on grounds that the trial was unjust.

Attorney Theodore Simon said he met last week in France with Ira Einhorn, a high-profile leader of Philadelphia's counterculture who was captured last month at his home in a renovated windmill after a 16-year international manhunt.

"At this point he wishes to contest the extradition, recognising that there are significant legal and international principles at stake that are even beyone this individual case," Simon said of Einhorn's intentions.
"You can anticipate that the issue of absentia will be fully and vigorously explored," Simon said.

Einhorn, 57, fled the United States in 1981 shortly before he was to go to trial on charges of killing his girlfriend in 1977. He had pleaded innocent to the killing, but was found guilty in 1993 and sentenced to life in prison after a trial at which he was not present.
An appeal by an earlier lawyer was rejected on the grounds Einhorn had forfeited his right to appeal by his absence.
A spokesman for the Philadelphia district attorney's office said an extradition request had been filed with the U.S. Justice Department and was likely to be presented to French authorities next week.
A Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling after Einhorn fled opened the door to a trial withough his presence.
A U.S.-French extradition treaty allows for the return within 40 days of the capture of a person wanted in the United States, spokesman Bill Davol said.

Trials in absentia are regarded by many countries and international treaties -- unsigned by the United States -- as violating basic legal rights, Simon said. Simon is a specialist in international law who has previously represented Americans abroad including Michael Fay, the teenager caned in Singapore as punishment for vandalism.

"In this (Einhorn) case, it really asks an important question: Can you have a trial, a meaningful one, if the defendant is not there and did not participate?" Simon said. "The French system will have to judge whether it will extradite someone who wasn't present" at his own trial.
Simon said France has denied extradition in past cases where a person has been tried in absentia. In addition, persons returned to France after a trial in absentia are granted new trials, he said.
Einhorn is being held by authorities in Bordeaux, France. Simon said Einhorn had reported being well-treated by his jailers and was in good spirits.
